## Why

[COR-1185](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1185>) ships the CLI's async path behind the layered `async_mirror_requests` setting, default off. This issue owns making async the normal CLI behavior — a released default change, deliberately separate from the implementation because a CLI release cannot be rolled back the way a traffic shift can. Per the decided shipping order, this follows the BFF path carrying real production traffic ([COR-1429](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1429>)).

## Observed facts

* The implementation (<pull-request id="76d249e5-9fec-4940-b271-8b565513f564" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/review/submit-mirror-creates-through-async-request-routes-3c7b89def3f4">entireio/cli#2207</pull-request>) is complete and parked as a draft; its issue records: no capability preflight, no 404 fallback, fail loudly; neutral async success output; the existing 2s/~30s phase-two poll tolerance absorbing the ~5s visibility 404.
* <issue id="e81d336f-8f51-4984-a32c-c8667c6e1319" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1185/cli-submit-mirror-creates-through-the-async-mirror-request-routes">COR-1185</issue>'s own criteria already require the pre-release validation runs (staging one-shot/`--no-wait`/wizard, then each prod region plus one wizard run, synthetic repos only) — those stay there; this issue starts after they pass.

## Proposed approach

Flip the setting's shipped default to async in a CLI release, after the <issue id="e81d336f-8f51-4984-a32c-c8667c6e1319" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1185/cli-submit-mirror-creates-through-the-async-mirror-request-routes">COR-1185</issue> validation matrix has passed and the BFF path has carried sustained production traffic. Record the release version here. Users can still opt back to the synchronous route via the layered setting until [COR-1207](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1207>) retires it.

Carried follow-up from [COR-1185](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1185>) (proposed, not settled): `--wait-timeout` has mode-specific semantics — the legacy sync route runs CreateMirror on the unbounded parent context and applies the timeout only to clone-readiness polling, while the async route uses one deadline across submission, placement, and clone polling. Sven dismissed changing this in <issue id="e81d336f-8f51-4984-a32c-c8667c6e1319" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1185/cli-submit-mirror-creates-through-the-async-mirror-request-routes">COR-1185</issue> as scope expansion for little value ([resolved review discussion](<https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2207#discussion_r3908821562>)). When this issue flips the default, the async semantics become what users see by default — either unify the behavior then, or document the mode split explicitly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The default resolves to the async route in a released CLI version, recorded here.
- [ ] The layered setting still allows opting back to the synchronous route.

name: task-implement
description: >
  Start and implement one well-scoped Linear or GitHub task: align it when
  needed, update native tracker state, run no-code work in a
  coordinator-workspace tab, or create an Entire worktree and focused
  implementation session when repository changes are required. Use Herdr when
  active; otherwise use the invoking session.
---

# Task Implementation

Move one well-scoped task from ready to active implementation while keeping the
tracker authoritative and the implementation context focused. Do not create an
Entire trail by default.

## Preflight

Before changing tracker state:

- Resolve the live task, repository, repository parent, current user, and task
  tracker access.
- Use Herdr enhancements only when `HERDR_ENV=1` and the Herdr CLI is available.
  Otherwise use the direct fallback; Herdr must not block the core workflow.

After preflight succeeds, assign the task to the user and move it to the
tracker's native in-progress state.

## Coordinator Working Directory

Record the directory where the coordinator started and keep its shell there for
the whole workflow. Do not use `cd` to navigate to the repository parent,
implementation worktree, or another task directory. Run repository-specific
commands with an explicit per-command working directory, a tool-native path
option such as `git -C`, or absolute paths. Give new Herdr tabs and workspaces
their required working directories at creation instead of moving the
coordinator. Change the coordinator's directory only when the user explicitly
asks.

## Choose Each Herdr Agent

Apply this immediately before every new `herdr agent start` performed by this
skill. Do not ask when resuming an existing live agent or when Herdr is absent.

Resolve the agent kind currently running this skill from the coordinator's live
Herdr agent. If it cannot be resolved, stop rather than guessing the timeout
default. After the role-specific workflow creates the destination tab and pane,
leave its shell idle. Use that shell to show a visible choice between Codex
(`codex`) and Claude Code (`claude`), focus the chooser, and send a Herdr
notification with the request sound. Wait up to 300 seconds for `c`/`codex` or
`l`/`claude`.

If the user does not answer within 300 seconds, select the coordinator's current
agent kind. An invalid answer does not select an agent; keep asking within the
original deadline. Have the shell print the selected canonical Herdr kind, wait
for the shell prompt to return, and pass that value to `herdr agent start
--kind`. The choice applies only to this dispatch; ask again before the next new
agent. Compare only the fixed accepted tokens; never evaluate the user's input
as shell text. Keep the timed read running in the destination pane and poll for
its result at intervals no longer than 60 seconds. Record each selected kind in
the live `Herdr peers` block, not the issue.

## Task Issue Ownership

The agent assigned to alignment, implementation, no-code execution, or guided
validation owns the task issue while doing that work. Include this ownership
contract in every task-agent handoff, with or without Herdr:

- Write durable task-local updates directly to the issue. This includes the
  approved alignment, verified implementation discoveries and decisions, and
  user-confirmed validation evidence. Do not send that content to the
  coordinator for transcription.
- Keep routine progress and conversation out of the issue. Post only information
  another person or later session needs to understand or continue the task.
- Do not change native project coordination state: assignment or workflow
  status, blocker or dependency relationships, milestones, project scope, or
  follow-up issue creation. Report those needs to the coordinator under the
  sparse messaging contract so it can reconcile the project.
- A user-approved edit to this task's body or exit criteria remains task-local
  unless it changes a dependency, milestone, project plan, or another task.

## Repository Task Lifecycle

Finishing the code is not finishing a repository task. "Implementation ready"
means the intended changes and directly related tests are complete, locally
verified, and reviewed under the selected Hunk boundary. Keep the task active
and the task agent responsible through the remaining lifecycle:

1. Create or update the pull request or Entire trail that carries the change.
2. Process every review round, address selected feedback, and obtain the
   required human or maintainer approval.
3. Land the approved change and deploy it to its intended environment.
4. Complete the agreed validation with evidence that is still current. The
   evidence may come from guided local validation, telemetry, or manual
   validation of the deployed behavior, as appropriate to the task.

If implementation or review changes behavior after validation, repeat the
affected validation before completion. Only when this lifecycle and the live
exit criteria are satisfied is the repository task complete. Earlier code,
review, pull-request, or validation milestones are durable task-local updates,
not completion reports to the coordinator. A no-code task is complete when its
own live exit criteria are satisfied.

## Herdr Peer Messaging

The coordinator channel is for task-state changes, not routine implementation
process. When Herdr is active, include this messaging contract in every agent's
initial prompt:

- Send one acknowledgment after accepting the handoff, naming the task and the
  current objective. Do not send periodic progress updates.
- Prompt the coordinator only when the task's native state may need to change:
  the complete repository-task lifecycle or a no-code task finishes; a blocker
  is expected to remain unresolved for several hours or beyond the current work
  session; an external dependency or coordinator authority is required; the
  agreed scope, exit criteria, dependency, rollout, milestone, or project plan
  needs to change; or newly discovered work requires another issue or project
  replanning. Do not report that implementation, review, a pull request, or an
  individual validation step finished.
- Keep code-review findings, Hunk comments, implementation choices, routine
  commit checkpoints, test or lint failures, local setup problems, and other
  transient blockers within the implementing agent's conversation with the
  user. Do not route those questions through the coordinator.
- If coordinator input is genuinely required, stop at a coherent boundary, say
  explicitly what task-state decision is awaited, and remain idle or blocked
  until the reply arrives. Do not keep working after sending the question.
- Send peer-to-peer handoffs directly to the agent that owns the next action;
  do not use the coordinator as a relay.
- Use `herdr agent prompt <target> "<message>"` for each qualifying
  acknowledgment, milestone, blocker, or handoff, using the exact live agent
  name or pane ID from the `Herdr peers` block.
- Use `herdr agent get <target>` if the target needs verification. Do not infer
  a target from tab order, UI focus, or terminal-multiplexer state.
- Never use `tmux`, raw pane input, or terminal key injection for peer messages.
- If Herdr rejects the target or prompt, do not fall back to another transport.
  Leave the error in the agent's response so the coordinator can resolve it.

The coordinator uses Herdr lifecycle state and read-only `herdr agent get` or
`herdr agent read` calls for rough visibility rather than requesting routine
updates. It does not turn implementation-local messages into user decisions or
reply to an agent that is still working. Before prompting an agent, verify that
it is idle or explicitly blocked waiting for coordinator input. A message
written only in one agent's terminal is not a handoff.

## Herdr References

Herdr's live IDs and labels are the source of truth. Give every workspace, tab,
and pane created by this skill a concise Herdr label at creation or immediately
afterward. Use the task `ID (title)` for the task workspace and role labels such
as `Alignment`, `Implementation`, `Shell`, and `Validation` for tabs and panes.
Do not maintain a separate name registry.

Before a human-facing report, chooser, handoff, or `Herdr peers` block, resolve
the current object with Herdr and render it as `ID (name)`, using the live Herdr
label as the name. Examples are
`w3 (COR-1185 Retry failed exports)`, `w3:t2 (Implementation)`, or
`w3:p4 (impl_cor-1185)`. For an agent pane, use the live Herdr agent name as the
parenthetical name. Do not substitute a bare role phrase such as “the
implementation tab” when the live object exists. If a pre-existing object is
unlabeled, use `ID (unlabeled)` rather than inventing a name or renaming a
user-owned object. Raw IDs remain appropriate in CLI arguments and machine
fields.

## Align

Use `pfleidi:task-align` unless the live task is already clear enough to execute
without first settling what work is being requested. Skip explicit alignment
only when all of these are true:

- The desired outcome, scope, exit criteria, and applicable validation are
  concrete and mutually consistent.
- Every exit criterion can be satisfied from existing prerequisites or state
  this task creates; none waits on later project work or unavailable traffic.
- Current evidence does not call the task's premise or requested change into
  question.
- Execution requires either no repository edits or only a few obvious code or
  configuration lines with no meaningful design choice.
- The task is not high-risk, destructive, broad, or dependent on a shared
  contract or maintenance direction that still needs agreement.

Operational validation, telemetry dashboard changes, small configuration
edits, well-scoped decision or investigation tasks, and similarly narrow work
commonly qualify. Their type alone is not enough: align when the issue leaves a
consequential prerequisite choice unresolved. Alignment should not perform the
decision or investigation that constitutes the task itself. When skipping
alignment, do not create an alignment tab, agent, or comment; use the live task
as the handoff and continue directly to path selection.

When running under Herdr, load its current agent instructions with
`herdr --skill`. Capture the coordinator workspace, tab, and pane from the
injected Herdr environment and resolve the current pane's live agent target.
Do not rely on UI focus.

Derive the applicable task agent names once. Lowercase the task ID, replace each
run of characters outside `[a-z0-9_-]` with `_`, prefix it with `align_`,
`task_`, or `impl_`, and truncate the complete name to 32
characters. Treat these as expected names: list live agents, reject ambiguous
collisions, and resume an existing name only after verifying that its pane and
workspace own this task. Do not add a suffix or create a registry file.

When alignment is required, create an ephemeral alignment tab in the
coordinator workspace with its working directory set to the repository parent.
Capture the returned tab and root-pane IDs, run the per-dispatch choice, and
start the alignment agent as `align_<task-id>` with the selected kind. Its
initial prompt must contain a `Herdr peers` block with:

- the task ID;
- the coordinator's actual agent or pane target, kind, and workspace
  `ID (name)`;
- the alignment agent's actual name, kind, tab `ID (name)`, and pane
  `ID (name)`;
- the expected no-code task and implementation names and roles.

Require the alignment agent to use `task-align`'s interactive brainstorming
loop. It must give the user the relevant system model, work through material
decisions with them, and confirm each decision before reporting alignment
ready. A bundled recommendation list followed by a blanket approval request is
not an alignment session.

Let the user conduct alignment in that tab. The alignment agent reports the
comment link and completion or a task-state blocker to the coordinator target.
The coordinator waits for the agent to settle and reads its output before
proceeding.
Keep the tab open while alignment is active or paused. For the code-change path,
keep it until implementation acknowledges the handoff; the no-code path closes
it as described below.

Without Herdr, perform required alignment in the invoking session. Skip tab
creation, peer-agent identity, and inter-agent communication.

If alignment shows that the task is blocked or not ready, do not create a
worktree. Reflect the outcome using the tracker's native state and the concise
alignment comment rather than a parallel status record.

## Choose The Execution Path

Use the live exit criteria and any alignment result to decide whether completion
requires repository edits and a commit. If the answer is unclear, run alignment
before creating a branch or worktree.

For a decision, investigation, tracker-only change, operational validation, or
other task that requires no repository change:

- Do not resolve a branch name, invoke Entire, create a worktree or task
  workspace, or start an implementation agent.
- Under Herdr, create a new tab in the existing coordinator workspace with its
  working directory set to the repository parent and label it for the task.
  Capture its returned tab and pane IDs and start a fresh `task_<task-id>` agent
  there using the per-dispatch agent choice. Do not create another workspace.
- Prompt that agent with the linked task `ID (title)`, the alignment comment
  when one exists, and a `Herdr peers` block containing the coordinator and no-code task agents'
  actual targets and kinds plus every workspace, tab, and pane as `ID (name)`,
  including the alignment agent when one was used.
  Require it to acknowledge the handoff to the coordinator before closing any
  alignment tab.
- Have the no-code task agent perform the work without editing repository files
  or creating commits, then report completion or a task-state blocker that meets
  the Herdr messaging threshold to the coordinator. The coordinator waits for
  it to settle and reads its output before closing the tab. Keep the tab open
  when user input is still required.
- Without Herdr, continue the work in the invoking session.
- In either path, use the issue's exit criteria as the completion contract.
- Persist durable findings and decisions in the issue, and use native tracker
  state for completion or follow-up work.

For an explicit staging or production validation task, exercise only supported
customer behavior: public API requests from a script, browser-driven web UI
flows, or normal CLI commands. Verify that the deployed system is wired
together and produces the customer-visible result. Do not connect to production
databases or internal services, inject faulty queue messages, manufacture
internal failures, or use privileged mechanisms unavailable to a customer.

Keep edge cases, failure injection, and critical correctness checks local and
prefer automated coverage executed in CI. If deployed validation exposes a
missing case that requires internal access to reproduce, record it and
reclassify the necessary automated test or code change rather than attempting
that case against staging or production.

Do not invoke `task-validate` for this path; it guides end-to-end validation of
an implemented repository change. If no-code work discovers that a code change
is required, stop, record the evidence, notify the coordinator, and reclassify
the task before entering the code-change path. Do not edit repository files
from the no-code tab.

## Telemetry Monitors

Every newly created telemetry monitor must reference a runbook. Search the
existing runbooks first and reuse one when it accurately covers the signal and
response. If none matches, create a runbook in the established location and
follow the structure and style of nearby runbooks. Do not create a duplicate
runbook merely to make it task-specific.

Treat the monitor and its runbook reference as one completion unit. When a new
runbook is needed, include it in the same implementation slice as the monitor.
If a task classified as no-code requires a repository runbook change, stop and
reclassify it before editing repository files.

## Prepare Code Work

Only when repository changes are required:

- Confirm the Entire CLI is available and the repository supports Entire
  worktrees.
- Look for an existing branch, worktree, pull request, or Entire trail for the
  task. Resume the matching work instead of creating a duplicate. If ownership
  or intent is unclear, stop with the conflicting evidence.
- For Linear, read and use the issue's suggested branch name exactly. For a
  GitHub issue without an existing or suggested branch, ask the user for the
  branch name instead of inventing a convention.
- Reject an empty or option-like branch name. Validate it with `git
  check-ref-format --branch`, then pass it to Entire as one quoted argument.

## Create The Implementation Worktree

For the code-change path, use Entire to create one worktree for the validated
task branch. `entire worktree create <branch>` creates and checks out a new
branch; use its existing-branch mode only when preparation established that the
matching branch already exists. Pass the branch as one quoted argument.

Do not use `git worktree`, create a trail, remove the implementation worktree,
or touch any other worktree. Record the path returned by Entire.

## Choose The Review Timing

Before editing repository files or starting an implementation agent, ask the
user to choose one review timing for this task. Recommend reviewing the
code-ready diff for a single coherent change expected to stay around
1,000 changed lines or less. Recommend reviewing before each commit for larger
work or changes that cross shared interfaces, schemas, dependencies, ownership
boundaries, security boundaries, persistence paths, or rollout behavior.

- **Review once code-ready:** Implement and verify the code as a sequence of
  small, focused commits without asking before each commit. The
  user's selection is explicit authorization to create only those local,
  in-scope commits. Once every code slice and its verification is complete,
  invoke `pfleidi:human-review` with branch scope so the user reviews the
  complete diff against `origin/main`.
- **Review before each commit:** Complete and verify one small behavior slice,
  then invoke `pfleidi:human-review` with slice scope. Commit only after the
  user approves that Hunk review, then begin the next slice. Do not run an
  additional branch review after the final slice unless the user asks for one.

Do not infer a mode from the selected agent, prior tasks, or repository history.
Reuse a mode only when the user already selected it for this exact task. If the
user has not selected a mode, do not edit or dispatch implementation.

Both modes require the same commit shape:

- Decompose the task into the smallest coherent behavior slices. Keep each
  slice's implementation and directly related tests together.
- Finish, verify, and commit each slice before starting the next. Never
  accumulate a multi-slice task into one uncommitted diff or one catch-all
  commit at the end.
- One commit is acceptable only when the entire task is itself one small,
  coherent, reviewable change.
- Stop for any unresolved material decision regardless of mode. Do not amend,
  push, open a pull request, or treat permission to create implementation
  commits as approval of the final implementation.

For review …759 tokens truncated…

When task work reveals a durable constraint, edge case, corrected fact, or
user-approved change of direction, the active task agent updates the relevant
issue field or adds a concise issue comment itself. It does not ask the
coordinator to copy the update. Start agent-generated handoff comments with the
required repository marker. Keep ordinary progress, branch state, and
pull-request state in their native tracker fields and links. Report any required
status, relationship, milestone, project-plan, or new-issue change to the
coordinator instead of applying it from the task agent.

Do not copy session conversation into the tracker. Never mention internal
session-capture configuration in generated issue output or handoffs.

## Tracker References

In human-facing prose, render every issue or pull request as `ID (title)` and
link the whole label when a URL exists. Never show a bare tracker ID or issue/PR
URL. Raw IDs remain valid in commands, API fields, branches, paths, and internal
identifiers.
---
name: testing
description: >
  Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope,
  avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go.
  Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing.
---

# Testing Guidance

## Core Principle

Tests should make changed behavior trustworthy without distorting production code. Prefer behavior and contracts over implementation details. Use the smallest scope that gives real confidence.

## Never Use Real Customer Data

**NEVER put real customer data in test cases.** No production records, real PII, real emails, real account/customer IDs, or scrubbed copies of live data — "anonymized" or "scrubbed" production data is still forbidden. Fabricate synthetic fixtures that exercise the same shape and edge cases. When reviewing, reject any test carrying real customer data outright.

## Choose Test Scope

- **Unit tests** - pure logic, parsing, validation, small components, and behavior with explicit dependencies that can be supplied naturally.
- **Integration tests** - real wiring, filesystem, config, databases, process boundaries, generated code, framework behavior, or cases where unit isolation would require awkward mocks or production-only seams.
- **End-to-end / smoke tests** - critical user or system flows across process or service boundaries. Keep these few, stable, and high value.

Cover changed behavior, important edge cases, and error paths. Do not chase line coverage with brittle tests that only exercise private structure.

## Preserve Test Layers

Unit, integration, and end-to-end suites are complementary layers with different costs. A fast unit suite may intentionally skip real wiring, config, databases, filesystems, generated code, or framework behavior when another suite owns that boundary. That is not incomplete unit testing; it is a useful split of responsibilities.

Before changing test scope, identify the missing confidence:

- If the gap is pure logic, parsing, validation, or small behavior with natural dependencies, add or adjust a unit test.
- If the gap is real wiring, config loading, filesystem/database behavior, generated code, process boundaries, or framework behavior, first check existing integration/e2e coverage. If coverage is missing, add a narrow integration/e2e test at that boundary.
- Preserve useful fast unit tests. Do not rewrite broad unit test suites into integration tests just to cover wiring. Convert a unit test only when its stated subject is wrong and an additive test at the right layer would not cover the gap.

## Avoid Production Test Seams

Do not add production code that exists only to make tests easier:

- Mutable function variables swapped in tests.
- Mutable package-wide settings changed by tests.
- Exported `Reset`, `Set`, or hook functions only used by tests.
- Global clocks, filesystems, HTTP clients, env readers, or command runners added only for unit tests.

If a test needs these, prefer dependency injection through existing construction paths, small typed interfaces around external effects, or a higher-scope integration test.

## Test Helpers

Helpers are useful when they make the test shorter and easier to understand. They are harmful when they hide the behavior being tested.

Use a helper when:

- It removes noisy setup or cleanup that is not the point of the test.
- Its name is domain-specific and explains what the caller gets.
- The test remains understandable without opening the helper.
- It preserves the important inputs, expected values, and assertions at the call site.

Inline the code instead when:

- The helper saves only a few lines but hides the arrange/act/assert flow.
- The reviewer must inspect the helper to know what behavior is asserted.
- The helper takes booleans, loose maps, or option bags that obscure intent.
- The helper embeds important defaults, expected values, or failure conditions.
- The helper is generic test plumbing with no domain meaning.

Prefer local helpers in the test file until reuse is clear. Moving helpers to shared test utilities raises the readability bar because future readers lose locality.

## Go-Specific Helper Rules

- Prefer table-driven tests or `t.Run` subtests when repeated cases share the same logic. Each table row should be a complete scenario with inputs, expected outputs, and a clear name.
- Keep expected values in the table row or test body. Do not hide them in helper defaults.
- Use `t.Run` names to identify cases, then keep failure messages focused on `got` vs `want`.
- If a helper can fail the test, accept `testing.TB` or `*testing.T` and call `t.Helper()` first so failures point to the caller.
- Use `t.Cleanup`, `t.TempDir`, and `t.Setenv` for resource setup when appropriate. Remember that process-wide changes such as environment or current-directory changes are not safe for parallel tests unless the testing API says so.
- Return concrete values from builders. Avoid global shared fixtures and mutable package state.
- Avoid generic assertion helpers unless they are clearly domain-specific. A direct `if got != want { t.Fatalf(...) }` is often more readable than an abstraction.

## Review Checklist

When writing or reviewing tests, flag:

- Changed behavior, edge cases, or error paths without meaningful coverage.
- Tests that prove private implementation details instead of behavior.
- Unit tests used where real wiring/config/filesystem/database/framework behavior is the confidence boundary.
- Review feedback that tries to replace useful unit tests with integration tests instead of adding a narrow integration/e2e test for a proven uncovered boundary.
- Helpers that force readers to leave the test to understand the scenario.
- Helpers that hide expected values, assertions, or important defaults.
- Production-only seams introduced to make tests pass.
- Broad mocks where an integration test would be simpler and more trustworthy.
- Real customer data in fixtures — production records, real PII, real IDs, or scrubbed copies of live data. Reject outright.

## Source Basis

This guidance is synthesized from Go's testing package documentation, Go's subtests guidance, and the Go table-driven tests wiki, plus local preferences about avoiding production-only test seams.

## Tracker References

In human-facing prose, render every issue or pull request as `ID (title)` and
link the whole label when a URL exists. Never show a bare tracker ID or issue/PR
URL. Raw IDs remain valid in commands, API fields, branches, paths, and internal
identifiers.

# Human Review

Give the user a stable diff to comprehend in Hunk, then coordinate the exact
human comments they select for action. This skill owns the review surface and
comment loop. It runs focused verification for edits made from review comments;
the invoking implementation or feedback workflow owns the final verification
boundary, commits, pushes, and remote publication.

Resolve the installed Hunk instructions with `hunk skill path` and read that
`SKILL.md` before using Hunk session commands. If Hunk is unavailable, stop and
report that local review cannot start.

## Require The Review Boundary

The invoking workflow must supply exactly one boundary. Do not choose or
recommend a boundary when this skill starts:

- **Slice**: review the stable uncommitted behavior slice against `HEAD` with
  `hunk diff --watch`. Use for review before each commit and for an uncommitted
  `pfleidi:feedback` fix batch.
- **Branch**: review the complete current branch and working tree against
  `origin/main` with `hunk diff --watch origin/main`. Use for a cohesive task
  only after implementation and its verification are complete.

`pfleidi:task-implement` chooses this boundary with the user before editing or
starting the implementation agent. `pfleidi:feedback` always supplies slice
scope for its uncommitted fix batch. For a standalone review of already
completed work, require the user to choose slice or branch scope explicitly. If
the boundary is missing or ambiguous, stop without opening or reloading Hunk.

Before opening Hunk, record the repository root, branch, `HEAD`, and working-tree
status. Require implementation edits to pause for the review. If `HEAD` changes
before the user finishes, reload the intended boundary and ask the user to
review the new candidate; do not apply comments against the stale candidate.

## Open Hunk

When `HERDR_ENV=1` and the Herdr CLI is available, read the current Herdr skill
with `herdr --skill` before controlling the session.

Use the implementation workspace ID supplied by `pfleidi:task-implement`. When
this skill runs inside that workspace, use `HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID`. Never infer the
workspace from UI focus or tab order. If Herdr is active but the implementation
workspace cannot be resolved, stop and report the missing ID.

Resolve the workspace, Hunk tab, and Hunk pane from Herdr before mentioning
them to the user. Render each as its live `ID (name)`, using the Herdr label as
the name, and label both objects created by this skill as `Hunk review`. Do not
replace the live reference with a bare phrase such as “the review tab.” If a
pre-existing object is unlabeled, use `ID (unlabeled)` rather than inventing a
name or renaming a user-owned object. Raw IDs remain appropriate in CLI
arguments and machine fields.

Create a tab labeled `Hunk review` in that workspace with its working directory
set to the implementation worktree, then launch the selected Hunk diff in its
root pane after labeling that pane `Hunk review`. Focus the tab because the user
requested an interactive review. On later reviews in the same implementation
workspace, reuse the single live
`Hunk review` tab and reload its Hunk session to the new boundary. If its Hunk
process has exited and the root pane is an idle shell, relaunch Hunk there. If
another foreground process owns that pane, or multiple tabs or sessions match,
report the relevant IDs and stop rather than guessing. Never close a review tab
created for the user.

Outside Herdr, do not launch an interactive command in the agent's terminal.
Give the user the exact `hunk diff` command for the selected boundary and wait
for them to open it. Once a session is live, use `hunk session` commands to
inspect and reload it.

After opening or relaunching Hunk, wait up to 10 seconds for
`hunk session list --json` to show a session whose repository root matches the
recorded implementation worktree. A running Hunk process and enabled agent
notes do not prove that the session has registered with the daemon. If a
sandboxed session query reports no sessions, retry it with localhost or network
escalation before treating the result as authoritative. Capture the matching
session ID and use that exact ID for every session command in the review pass;
resolve it again after any relaunch.

If an escalated query still shows no matching session after the bounded wait,
do not repeat comment commands, substitute another repository path, or infer a
session from the running process. Keep the review surface open, report that the
TUI has not registered with the daemon, and ask the user before relaunching it
because a relaunch can discard review state.

## Process Human Comments

Snapshot the existing user-comment IDs when the review opens or reloads, then
wait until the user says the review is complete. A request such as “address all
current user comments in Hunk” explicitly selects the comments added since that
snapshot. Include an older comment only when the user selects it by ID or exact
text. Without that selection, list the comments but do not edit code.

Before editing:

1. Read `hunk session comment list <session-id> --type user --json` and isolate
   the selected IDs from the review's opening snapshot.
2. Present every selected comment verbatim with its file and line, current-code
   relevance, and the intended response.
3. Continue with independent unambiguous comments. Ask for the exact decision
   on comments that change behavior, contracts, scope, risk, test strategy, or
   have more than one reasonable response.

Apply selected comments at the narrowest correct level. Keep directly related
tests with behavior changes, then run focused verification for the changed
surface. Do not commit, push, clear human comments, or mark the review approved.
Return the verification evidence to the invoking workflow so it can reuse a
still-current result, then reload the Hunk session so the user can inspect the
result. Report each comment as addressed, unchanged with reason, or waiting on
a named decision. Treat the current comment IDs as the opening snapshot for the
next pass. Repeat until the user approves the review or leaves no selected
comments.

---
name: task-implement
description: >
  Start and implement one well-scoped Linear or GitHub task: align it when
  needed, update native tracker state, run no-code work in a
  coordinator-workspace tab, or create an Entire worktree and focused
  implementation session when repository changes are required. Use Herdr when
  active; otherwise use the invoking session.
---

# Task Implementation

Move one well-scoped task from ready to active implementation while keeping the
tracker authoritative and the implementation context focused. Do not create an
Entire trail by default.

## Preflight

Before changing tracker state:

- Resolve the live task, repository, repository parent, current user, and task
  tracker access.
- Use Herdr enhancements only when `HERDR_ENV=1` and the Herdr CLI is available.
  Otherwise use the direct fallback; Herdr must not block the core workflow.

After preflight succeeds, assign the task to the user and move it to the
tracker's native in-progress state.

## Coordinator Working Directory

Record the directory where the coordinator started and keep its shell there for
the whole workflow. Do not use `cd` to navigate to the repository parent,
implementation worktree, or another task directory. Run repository-specific
commands with an explicit per-command working directory, a tool-native path
option such as `git -C`, or absolute paths. Give new Herdr tabs and workspaces
their required working directories at creation instead of moving the
coordinator. Change the coordinator's directory only when the user explicitly
asks.

## Choose Each Herdr Agent

Apply this immediately before every new `herdr agent start` performed by this
skill. Do not ask when resuming an existing live agent or when Herdr is absent.

Resolve the agent kind currently running this skill from the coordinator's live
Herdr agent. If it cannot be resolved, stop rather than guessing the timeout
default. After the role-specific workflow creates the destination tab and pane,
leave its shell idle. Use that shell to show a visible choice between Codex
(`codex`) and Claude Code (`claude`), focus the chooser, and send a Herdr
notification with the request sound. Wait up to 300 seconds for `c`/`codex` or
`l`/`claude`.

If the user does not answer within 300 seconds, select the coordinator's current
agent kind. An invalid answer does not select an agent; keep asking within the
original deadline. Have the shell print the selected canonical Herdr kind, wait
for the shell prompt to return, and pass that value to `herdr agent start
--kind`. The choice applies only to this dispatch; ask again before the next new
agent. Compare only the fixed accepted tokens; never evaluate the user's input
as shell text. Keep the timed read running in the destination pane and poll for
its result at intervals no longer than 60 seconds. Record each selected kind in
the live `Herdr peers` block, not the issue.

## Task Issue Ownership

The agent assigned to alignment, implementation, no-code execution, or guided
validation owns the task issue while doing that work. Include this ownership
contract in every task-agent handoff, with or without Herdr:

- Write durable task-local updates directly to the issue. This includes the
  approved alignment, verified implementation discoveries and decisions, and
  user-confirmed validation evidence. Do not send that content to the
  coordinator for transcription.
- Keep routine progress and conversation out of the issue. Post only information
  another person or later session needs to understand or continue the task.
- Do not change native project coordination state: assignment or workflow
  status, blocker or dependency relationships, milestones, project scope, or
  follow-up issue creation. Report those needs to the coordinator under the
  sparse messaging contract so it can reconcile the project.
- A user-approved edit to this task's body or exit criteria remains task-local
  unless it changes a dependency, milestone, project plan, or another task.

## Repository Task Lifecycle

Finishing the code is not finishing a repository task. "Implementation ready"
means the intended changes and directly related tests are complete, locally
verified, and reviewed under the selected Hunk boundary. Keep the task active
and the task agent responsible through the remaining lifecycle:

1. Create or update the pull request or Entire trail that carries the change.
2. Process every review round, address selected feedback, and obtain the
   required human or maintainer approval.
3. Land the approved change and deploy it to its intended environment.
4. Complete the agreed validation with evidence that is still current. The
   evidence may come from guided local validation, telemetry, or manual
   validation of the deployed behavior, as appropriate to the task.

If implementation or review changes behavior after validation, repeat the
affected validation before completion. Only when this lifecycle and the live
exit criteria are satisfied is the repository task complete. Earlier code,
review, pull-request, or validation milestones are durable task-local updates,
not completion reports to the coordinator. A no-code task is complete when its
own live exit criteria are satisfied.

## Herdr Peer Messaging

The coordinator channel is for task-state changes, not routine implementation
process. When Herdr is active, include this messaging contract in every agent's
initial prompt:

- Send one acknowledgment after accepting the handoff, naming the task and the
  current objective. Do not send periodic progress updates.
- Prompt the coordinator only when the task's native state may need to change:
  the complete repository-task lifecycle or a no-code task finishes; a blocker
  is expected to remain unresolved for several hours or beyond the current work
  session; an external dependency or coordinator authority is required; the
  agreed scope, exit criteria, dependency, rollout, milestone, or project plan
  needs to change; or newly discovered work requires another issue or project
  replanning. Do not report that implementation, review, a pull request, or an
  individual validation step finished.
- Keep code-review findings, Hunk comments, implementation choices, routine
  commit checkpoints, test or lint failures, local setup problems, and other
  transient blockers within the implementing agent's conversation with the
  user. Do not route those questions through the coordinator.
- If coordinator input is genuinely required, stop at a coherent boundary, say
  explicitly what task-state decision is awaited, and remain idle or blocked
  until the reply arrives. Do not keep working after sending the question.
- Send peer-to-peer handoffs directly to the agent that owns the next action;
  do not use the coordinator as a relay.
- Use `herdr agent prompt <target> "<message>"` for each qualifying
  acknowledgment, milestone, blocker, or handoff, using the exact live agent
  name or pane ID from the `Herdr peers` block.
- Use `herdr agent get <target>` if the target needs verification. Do not infer
  a target from tab order, UI focus, or terminal-multiplexer state.
- Never use `tmux`, raw pane input, or terminal key injection for peer messages.
- If Herdr rejects the target or prompt, do not fall back to another transport.
  Leave the error in the agent's response so the coordinator can resolve it.

The coordinator uses Herdr lifecycle state and read-only `herdr agent get` or
`herdr agent read` calls for rough visibility rather than requesting routine
updates. It does not turn implementation-local messages into user decisions or
reply to an agent that is still working. Before prompting an agent, verify that
it is idle or explicitly blocked waiting for coordinator input. A message
written only in one agent's terminal is not a handoff.

## Herdr References

Herdr's live IDs and labels are the source of truth. Give every workspace, tab,
and pane created by this skill a concise Herdr label at creation or immediately
afterward. Use the task `ID (title)` for the task workspace and role labels such
as `Alignment`, `Implementation`, `Shell`, and `Validation` for tabs and panes.
Do not maintain a separate name registry.

Before a human-facing report, chooser, handoff, or `Herdr peers` block, resolve
the current object with Herdr and render it as `ID (name)`, using the live Herdr
label as the name. Examples are

For a decision, investigation, tracker-only change, operational validation, or
other task that requires no repository change:

- Do not resolve a branch name, invoke Entire, create a worktree or task
  workspace, or start an implementation agent.
- Under Herdr, create a new tab in the existing coordinator workspace with its
  working directory set to the repository parent and label it for the task.
  Capture its returned tab and pane IDs and start a fresh `task_<task-id>` agent
  there using the per-dispatch agent choice. Do not create another workspace.
- Prompt that agent with the linked task `ID (title)`, the alignment comment
  when one exists, and a `Herdr peers` block containing the coordinator and no-code task agents'
  actual targets and kinds plus every workspace, tab, and pane as `ID (name)`,
  including the alignment agent when one was used.
  Require it to acknowledge the handoff to the coordinator before closing any
  alignment tab.
- Have the no-code task agent perform the work without editing repository files
  or creating commits, then report completion or a task-state blocker that meets
  the Herdr messaging threshold to the coordinator. The coordinator waits for
  it to settle and reads its output before closing the tab. Keep the tab open
  when user input is still required.
- Without Herdr, continue the work in the invoking session.
- In either path, use the issue's exit criteria as the completion contract.
- Persist durable findings and decisions in the issue, and use native tracker
  state for completion or follow-up work.

For an explicit staging or production validation task, exercise only supported
customer behavior: public API requests from a script, browser-driven web UI
flows, or normal CLI commands. Verify that the deployed system is wired
together and produces the customer-visible result. Do not connect to production
databases or internal services, inject faulty queue messages, manufacture
internal failures, or use privileged mechanisms unavailable to a customer.

Keep edge cases, failure injection, and critical correctness checks local and
prefer automated coverage executed in CI. If deployed validation exposes a
missing case that requires internal access to reproduce, record it and
reclassify the necessary automated test or code change rather than attempting
that case against staging or production.

Do not invoke `task-validate` for this path; it guides end-to-end validation of
an implemented repository change. If no-code work discovers that a code change
is required, stop, record the evidence, notify the coordinator, and reclassify
the task before entering the code-change path. Do not edit repository files
from the no-code tab.

## Telemetry Monitors

Every newly created telemetry monitor must reference a runbook. Search the
existing runbooks first and reuse one when it accurately covers the signal and
response. If none matches, create a runbook in the established location and
follow the structure and style of nearby runbooks. Do not create a duplicate
runbook merely to make it task-specific.

Treat the monitor and its runbook reference as one completion unit. When a new
runbook is needed, include it in the same implementation slice as the monitor.
If a task classified as no-code requires a repository runbook change, stop and
reclassify it before editing repository files.

## Prepare Code Work

Only when repository changes are required:

- Confirm the Entire CLI is available and the repository supports Entire
  worktrees.
- Look for an existing branch, worktree, pull request, or Entire trail for the
  task. Resume the matching work instead of creating a duplicate. If ownership

# Task Implementation

Move one well-scoped task from ready to active implementation while keeping the
tracker authoritative and the implementation context focused. Do not create an
Entire trail by default.

## Preflight

Before changing tracker state:

- Resolve the live task, repository, repository parent, current user, and task
  tracker access.
- Use Herdr enhancements only when `HERDR_ENV=1` and the Herdr CLI is available.
  Otherwise use the direct fallback; Herdr must not block the core workflow.

After preflight succeeds, assign the task to the user and move it to the
tracker's native in-progress state.

## Coordinator Working Directory

Record the directory where the coordinator started and keep its shell there for
the whole workflow. Do not use `cd` to navigate to the repository parent,
implementation worktree, or another task directory. Run repository-specific
commands with an explicit per-command working directory, a tool-native path
option such as `git -C`, or absolute paths. Give new Herdr tabs and workspaces
their required working directories at creation instead of moving the
coordinator. Change the coordinator's directory only when the user explicitly
asks.

## Choose Each Herdr Agent

Apply this immediately before every new `herdr agent start` performed by this
skill. Do not ask when resuming an existing live agent or when Herdr is absent.

Resolve the agent kind currently running this skill from the coordinator's live
Herdr agent. If it cannot be resolved, stop rather than guessing the timeout
default. After the role-specific workflow creates the destination tab and pane,
leave its shell idle. Use that shell to show a visible choice between Codex
(`codex`) and Claude Code (`claude`), focus the chooser, and send a Herdr
notification with the request sound. Wait up to 300 seconds for `c`/`codex` or
`l`/`claude`.

If the user does not answer within 300 seconds, select the coordinator's current
agent kind. An invalid answer does not select an agent; keep asking within the
original deadline. Have the shell print the selected canonical Herdr kind, wait
for the shell prompt to return, and pass that value to `herdr agent start
--kind`. The choice applies only to this dispatch; ask again before the next new
agent. Compare only the fixed accepted tokens; never evaluate the user's input
as shell text. Keep the timed read running in the destination pane and poll for
its result at intervals no longer than 60 seconds. Record each selected kind in
the live `Herdr peers` block, not the issue.

## Task Issue Ownership

The agent assigned to alignment, implementation, no-code execution, or guided
validation owns the task issue while doing that work. Include this ownership
contract in every task-agent handoff, with or without Herdr:

- Write durable task-local updates directly to the issue. This includes the
  approved alignment, verified implementation discoveries and decisions, and
  user-confirmed validation evidence. Do not send that content to the
  coordinator for transcription.
- Keep routine progress and conversation out of the issue. Post only information
  another person or later session needs to understand or continue the task.
- Do not change native project coordination state: assignment or workflow
  status, blocker or dependency relationships, milestones, project scope, or
  follow-up issue creation. Report those needs to the coordinator under the
  sparse messaging contract so it can reconcile the project.
- A user-approved edit to this task's body or exit criteria remains task-local
  unless it changes a dependency, milestone, project plan, or another task.

## Repository Task Lifecycle

Finishing the code is not finishing a repository task. "Implementation ready"
means the intended changes and directly related tests are complete, locally
verified, and reviewed under the selected Hunk boundary. Keep the task active
and the task agent responsible through the remaining lifecycle:

1. Create or update the pull request or Entire trail that carries the change.
2. Process every review round, address selected feedback, and obtain the
   required human or maintainer approval.
3. Land the approved change and deploy it to its intended environment.
4. Complete the agreed validation with evidence that is still current. The
   evidence may come from guided local validation, telemetry, or manual
   validation of the deployed behavior, as appropriate to the task.

If implementation or review changes behavior after validation, repeat the
affected validation before completion. Only when this lifecycle and the live
exit criteria are satisfied is the repository task complete. Earlier code,
review, pull-request, or validation milestones are durable task-local updates,
not completion reports to the coordinator. A no-code task is complete when its
own live exit criteria are satisfied.

## Herdr Peer Messaging

The coordinator channel is for task-state changes, not routine implementation
process. When Herdr is active, include this messaging contract in every agent's
initial prompt:

- Send one acknowledgment after accepting the handoff, naming the task and the
  current objective. Do not send periodic progress updates.
- Prompt the coordinator only when the task's native state may need to change:
  the complete repository-task lifecycle or a no-code task finishes; a blocker
  is expected to remain unresolved for several hours or beyond the current work

  agreed scope, exit criteria, dependency, rollout, milestone, or project plan

  replanning. Do not report that implementation, review, a pull request, or an
  individual validation step finished.

  commit checkpoints, test or lint failures, local setup problems, and other
  transient blockers within the implementing agent's conversation with the
  user. Do not route those questions through the coordinator.

  explicitly what task-state decision is awaited, and remain idle or blocked

  do not use the coordinator as a relay.

name: herdr
description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` means the agent is ready for input and its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI. `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work finishes. Focusing the tab or targeting the pane or agent with a focus command marks it seen. CLI reads do not mark it seen. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter after a short delay. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

A prompt sent from a non-working state must produce an observed lifecycle change within five seconds. Otherwise Herdr returns `agent_prompt_stalled` instead of waiting indefinitely. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` atomically sends command text and Enter. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. If increasing it does not reveal more of a completed response, the pane is probably running the agent on the terminal's alternate screen. Rows that leave the alternate screen do not enter Herdr's host scrollback, so a larger line count cannot recover them.

After that failed read, ask the agent to write its complete response as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read the file directly. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

---
name: hunk-review
description: Interacts with live Hunk diff review sessions via CLI. Inspects review focus, navigates files, hunks, and exact lines, reloads session contents, adds inline review comments, and paints attention marks on character ranges. Use when the user has a Hunk session running or wants to review diffs interactively.
---

# Hunk Review

Hunk is an interactive terminal diff viewer. The TUI is for the user -- do NOT run `hunk diff`, `hunk show`, or other interactive commands directly. Use `hunk session *` CLI commands to inspect and control live sessions through the local daemon.

If no session exists, ask the user to launch Hunk in their terminal first.

## Workflow

```text
1. hunk session list                                    # find live sessions
2. hunk session get --repo .                            # inspect path / repo / source
3. hunk session review --repo . --json                  # inspect file/hunk structure first
4. hunk session review --repo . --include-patch --json  # opt into raw diff text only when needed
5. hunk session context --repo .                        # check current focus when needed
6. hunk session navigate ...                            # move to the right place
7. hunk session reload -- <command>                     # swap contents if needed
8. hunk session comment add ...                         # leave one review note
9. hunk session comment apply ...                       # apply many agent notes in one stdin batch
10. hunk session highlight add ...                      # light up the exact range you are explaining
```

## Session selection

Most session commands accept:

- `--repo <path>` -- match the live session by its current loaded repo root (most common)
- `<session-id>` -- match by exact ID (use when multiple sessions share a repo)
- If only one session exists, it auto-resolves

`reload` also supports:

- `--session-path <path>` -- match the live Hunk window by its current working directory
- `--source <path>` -- load the replacement `diff` / `show` command from a different directory

Use `--source` only for advanced reloads where the live session you want to control is not already associated with the checkout you want to load next. For a normal worktree session, prefer selecting it directly with `--repo /path/to/worktree`.

## Commands

### Inspect

```bash
hunk session list [--json]
hunk session get (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session context (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session review (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--include-patch] [--include-notes] [--json]
```

- `get` shows the session `Path`, `Repo`, and `Source`, which helps when choosing between `--repo` and `--session-path`
- `Repo` is what `--repo` matches; `Path` is what `--session-path` matches
- `review --json` returns file and hunk structure by default; add `--include-patch` only when a caller truly needs raw unified diff text
- `review --include-notes` also returns the live review notes alongside the file and hunk structure

### Navigate

```bash
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--hunk <n> | --old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) [--json]
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) (--next-comment | --prev-comment) [--json]
```

Absolute navigation requires `--file` and exactly one of `--hunk`, `--new-line`, or `--old-line`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --hunk 2
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 372
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --old-line 355
```

Relative comment navigation jumps between annotated hunks and does not require `--file`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --next-comment
hunk session navigate --repo . --prev-comment
```

- `--hunk <n>` is 1-based
- `--new-line` / `--old-line` are 1-based line numbers on that diff side
- A line target lands the user's viewport on that exact line (falling back to its hunk when the line is inside a collapsed region); `--hunk` lands on the hunk
- Use either `--next-comment` or `--prev-comment`, not both

### Reload

Swaps the live session's contents. Pass a Hunk review command after `--`:

```bash
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- diff [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- show [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff main...feature -- src/ui
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1 -- README.md
hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff
hunk session reload --session-path /path/to/live-window --source /path/to/other-checkout -- diff
```

- Always include `--` before the nested Hunk command
- `--repo` or `<session-id>` usually selects the session you want
- `--source` is advanced: it does not select the session; it only changes where the replacement review command runs
- If the live session is already showing the target worktree, prefer `hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff`
- `--session-path` targets the live window when you need to keep session selection separate from reload source

### Comments

```bash
hunk session comment add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --summary <text> [--rationale <text>] [--author <name>] [--markup <stml>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment apply (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --stdin [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment list (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--type <live|all|ai|agent|user>] [--json]
hunk session comment rm (<session-id> | --repo <path>) <comment-id> [--json]
hunk session comment clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--include-user|--all] --yes [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session comment add --repo . --file README.md --new-line 103 --summary "Tighten this wording"
printf '%s\n' '{"comments":[{"filePath":"README.md","newLine":103,"summary":"Tighten this wording"}]}' | hunk session comment apply --repo . --stdin
```

- `comment list --type user` shows human-authored inline notes; without `--type`, `comment list` preserves the legacy live-agent-comment view
- `comment add` is best for one note; `comment apply` is best when an agent already has several notes ready
- `comment add` requires `--file`, `--summary`, and exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`
- `comment apply` payload items require `filePath`, `summary`, and exactly one target such as `hunk`, `hunkNumber`, `oldLine`, or `newLine`
- `comment apply` reads a JSON batch from stdin and validates the full batch before mutating the live session
- Pass `--focus` when you want to jump to the new note or the first note in a batch
- `comment list` and `comment clear` accept optional `--file`
- Quote `--summary` and `--rationale` defensively in the shell

### Attention marks

Highlights paint character ranges inside the diff lines the user is looking at — use them to light up the exact expression you are explaining while you narrate.

```bash
hunk session highlight add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --start <n> --end <n> [--tone <tone>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session highlight clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19 --tone warning --focus
hunk session highlight clear --repo .
```

- `highlight add` requires `--file`, exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`, and the `--start` / `--end` offsets
- `--start` is a 0-based inclusive offset into the line's text and `--end` is exclusive, counted in UTF-16 code units — the same `[start, end)` range extensions use
- Tones: `match` (default), `info`, `warning`, `error`; `current` renders as reverse video and is best reserved for the one range under discussion
- Pass `--focus` to also land the viewport on the marked line
- Marks survive scrolling, navigation, and reloads that leave the marked file's content unchanged; a reload that changes that file drops its marks, and `highlight clear` removes them explicitly (optionally per `--file`)
- Marks are visual only — pair them with a `comment add` when the explanation should persist as a note

### Experimental rich markup notes (STML)

Only use STML when `hunk session context --json` lists `stml` in `experimentalFeatures`. The user opts into that experience by launching the review with `--experimental`; do not ask a normal session to render markup.

For an opted-in session, `--markup` (or a `markup` field on apply items) renders the note body as STML — a small HTML-like markup for terminal UI (boxes, rows, gauges, badges, lists, code). Keep `--summary` a real sentence: it is the fallback and the `comment list` text.

Before writing markup, run `hunk markup guide` once — it has copy-paste patterns and the width rules. The session context also reports `noteMarkupWidth` (the live render width); preview with `hunk markup render - --width <that>`.
